strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 20+ diverse tasks (MuJoCo, ManiSkill state/RGB) with consistent improvements (1.3-1.9x sample efficiency gains on several tasks) and proper statistical reporting (5 seeds, 95% confidence intervals)

Solid theoretical contribution: Proposition 4.1 rigorously analyzes gradient variance differences between Gaussian and categorical policies with tight bounds; provides useful intuition despite simplified toy setting

Thorough ablation studies effectively isolate design choices: loss-swap ablation (Figure 6b) elegantly shows cross-entropy vs squared error is critical, component analysis validates each architectural choice, and bin granularity sweep reveals sensitivity

Clear presentation and well-motivated approach: The paper articulates compelling analogy between cross-entropy success in value learning and its application to policy optimization; writing is accessible and logical flow is strong

Strong reproducibility: Comprehensive hyperparameters (Table 1), detailed environment specifications (Appendix B.2), complete learning curves, and use of established codebases (CleanRL, ManiSkill) enable easy reproduction

Principled experimental design: Fair comparisons with identical critic architecture across variants; systematic component analysis showing residual connections and layer norm each contribute independently
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: Discretized categorical policies already explored by Tang & Agrawal (2020) and Zhu et al. (2024); regularized architectures (residual blocks with layer norm) are standard in modern ML and prior RL work (SimBa, BroNet). Main contribution is demonstrating their combination works well—an engineering contribution more than a fundamental algorithmic advance

Narrow algorithmic scope: All experiments use PPO only with no evaluation of other on-policy methods (TRPO, A3C, A2C, newer variants), limiting generalizability of findings despite claims of contributing to 'on-policy RL' broadly

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: Proposition 4.1 assumes constant return and vanilla REINFORCE, yet realistic PPO uses advantage baselines, clipping, and GAE normalization—applicability gap remains unclear. Missing analysis of why regularization specifically helps categorical policies or their interaction

Lack of principled hyperparameter guidance: Performance highly sensitive to bin count (Figure 6d) with substantial degradation beyond optimal K; no principled method for selecting K across task types or action dimensionalities. K=41 choice appears arbitrary and task-dependent

Oversimplified cross-entropy analysis (Section 4.2): Comparison assumes fixed Σ = σ²I for Gaussian, but many implementations learn variance; doesn't explain why cross-entropy specifically improves optimization beyond variance reduction; lacks bias-variance tradeoff discussion between discretization and continuous approximation

Mixed performance vs. strong baselines and statistical concerns: Wall-clock comparisons vs TD3/TD-MPC2 show inconsistent advantages (outperforms on StackCube but less efficient on Humanoid); some improvements have overlapping confidence intervals (e.g., HalfCheetah) without explicit significance testing

Limited analysis of failure modes and real-world applicability: No discussion of when discretized categorical policies are inappropriate (very high-dimensional actions, continuous fine-grained control), computational overhead, or guidance for scaling to different action spaces; all tasks are simulated benchmarks

strengths: Clear conceptual framing connecting categorical policies to cross-entropy objectives with good intuitive appeal
Rigorous theoretical analysis (Proposition 4.1) formalizing gradient variance differences between policy families with sound proofs
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three diverse benchmark families (20 total tasks) with consistent improvements
Thorough ablation studies including loss-swap ablation (C.2) that isolates the objective's role and component analysis showing SNR-performance correlation
Strong reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, established baseline implementations, 5 random seeds with confidence intervals
Practical improvements demonstrated (1.3-1.9× sample efficiency gains, successful solutions on challenging tasks like StackCube)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: discretized categorical policies (Tang & Agrawal 2020, Zhu et al. 2024) and regularized architectures (residual blocks, LayerNorm from SimBa/BroNet/Transformers) are existing ideas; contribution is primarily combining pre-existing components

Confounded contribution: simultaneously changes policy parameterization and actor architecture without cleanly separating their effects; vision-based results show the gap narrows with good encoders (CNN), suggesting architecture drives improvements as much as discretization

Theory-practice gap: Proposition 4.1 assumes fixed state, constant return, and vanilla REINFORCE—far removed from actual PPO with clipping, advantage estimation, and multi-epoch updates; no connection established between reduced variance and performance in realistic settings

Significant hyperparameter sensitivity (Appendix C.4): performance degrades sharply as bins increase, reaching near-baseline with K=1001; suggests benefits may stem from coarse discretization's inductive bias rather than cross-entropy objective; no principled bin selection method provided

Incomplete characterization of when method works: gains vary widely across tasks (small on Hopper/HalfCheetah, large on StackCube, minimal on vision-based); no analysis of what task properties determine effectiveness

Loss-swap ablation ambiguity: while showing cross-entropy importance, doesn't prove it's the driver—the discretized representation combined with MSE may simply create a worse landscape; doesn't isolate discretization independently
Limited SOTA comparisons: TD3/TD-MPC2 comparison only on 2 tasks with wall-clock time on different hardware; main comparisons are against standard PPO MLP baselines, not recent on-policy variants

No theoretical justification for architectural choices: why do residual connections and LayerNorm specifically suit categorical policies? Paper acknowledges borrowing from prior work but doesn't explain particular suitability
Statistical rigor gaps: no formal significance testing despite some per-task improvements lying within confidence intervals; aggregate speedup (1.3-1.9×) hides substantial task-level variability

Scope limitations: only evaluated on PPO (future work to try other algorithms), only continuous control, only standard benchmarks; no evaluation on Beta/Bernoulli distributions mentioned in related work

strengths: Strong empirical results across diverse benchmarks (20+ tasks) with consistent improvements and 1.3-1.9× sample efficiency gains, validated over 5 seeds with proper confidence intervals

Clear gradient variance analysis (Proposition 4.1) showing categorical policies have bounded variance while Gaussian variance grows unboundedly as exploration decreases, empirically validated in Figure 4

Comprehensive and well-designed ablations including critical loss-swap experiment (Figure 6b) isolating the role of cross-entropy optimization, component analysis, and sensitivity studies on network capacity and bin counts
Excellent performance on challenging manipulation tasks (notably StackCube-v1 where RN-D is the only method achieving reliable high success), demonstrating practical utility
Well-structured presentation with clear motivation connecting actor design to cross-entropy classification-style losses, intuitive framing, and high-quality figures and experimental documentation
weaknesses: Limited novelty in individual components: discretized categorical actors exist in prior work (Tang & Agrawal 2020, Zhu et al. 2024), and regularized residual MLPs with layer norm follow established patterns from SimBa, BroNet, and Transformers. Contribution is primarily empirical validation of combining these existing ideas rather than conceptual innovation

Theoretical analysis (Proposition 4.1) is limited to toy setting with vanilla REINFORCE and constant returns, far from PPO's importance weighting and advantage clipping. No convergence guarantees or optimality analysis. Connection between cross-entropy losses and supervised learning architecture benefits is intuitive but not rigorously justified

Bin count sensitivity (Appendix C.4) shows substantial performance degradation with large K, with no principled guidance for selecting K. Performance decreases logarithmically with bin count on StackCube, limiting scalability to high-dimensional action spaces and contradicting claims of improved scalability

Confounded design choices make it difficult to isolate improvement sources: RN-D differs from MLP-C in both discretization and architecture; RN-C already shows gains over MLP-C suggesting architecture partially responsible; regularized network brings MLP-C close to RN-D on vision tasks

Limited understanding of when discrete actors should be applied: improvements vary significantly across task types (large on manipulation, modest on locomotion); no characterization of task properties favoring the approach; why StackCube shows dramatic improvements is unexplained, limiting practitioners' ability to apply method

Baseline comparison concerns: critic networks use different activation functions across settings (Tanh vs ReLU); no evidence baselines received comparable hyperparameter tuning; TD3/TD-MPC2 comparisons limited to 2 tasks; missing comparisons to Beta distribution and recent unimodal discrete parameterizations despite relevant prior work

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across diverse benchmarks (Gym locomotion, ManiSkill state/vision), algorithms (PPO, TRPO, SPO), with consistent improvements of 1.3-1.9× sample efficiency
Well-designed ablations, particularly the loss-swap ablation isolating the role of cross-entropy vs. squared-error objectives, showing discretization alone is insufficient
Clear motivation connecting on-policy actor updates to classification-style objectives with rigorous gradient variance analysis (Proposition 4.1) showing categorical policies have lower variance
Algorithm-agnostic generality: consistent improvements across three different on-policy algorithms demonstrates robustness
Strong reproducibility practices including promised code release, complete hyperparameter specifications, 5 random seeds with bootstrap confidence intervals, and extensive appendices
Practical value with meaningful sample efficiency gains and no runtime overhead (Table 1), making this an actionable drop-in replacement
Thorough extended studies including scaling analysis (actor width, bin count), runtime analysis, gradient signal-to-noise ratio analysis showing strong correlation with performance
weaknesses: Limited novelty: combines three existing techniques (discrete categorical policies from Tang & Agrawal 2020; regularized MLPs from SimBa/BroNet; cross-entropy loss comparison from distributional RL) without introducing fundamentally new methods
Modest theoretical contributions: Proposition 4.1 is correct but relatively straightforward, following directly from basic probability without deeper insights into optimization implications
Mixed results for vision-based tasks: performance improvements are notably smaller for RGB-based ManiSkill tasks (Figure 4), suggesting the benefits may be domain-specific

Sensitivity to discretization granularity: performance degrades sharply with large K values (Figure 8d), introducing a new hyperparameter to tune and contradicting claims of being a simple drop-in replacement
Limited experimental scope: only continuous control on standard benchmarks, no high-dimensional action spaces (>20D), and only state/pixel observations; generalization unclear
Actor-critic interaction unexplored: critic kept fixed by design, preventing understanding of joint scaling or complementary architectural choices
Hyperparameter sensitivity concern: while using defaults aids reproducibility, PPO is known to be hyperparameter-sensitive; unclear if improvements hold under task-specific tuning
Claim of 'state-of-the-art within on-policy RL' is somewhat overstated; limited comparison to other on-policy methods and performance advantage over TD3 is mixed (Appendix C.1)

strengths: Consistent empirical improvements across multiple on-policy algorithms (PPO, TRPO, SPO) and diverse benchmarks with fair ablation comparisons
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple seeds, confidence intervals, runtime analysis, and extended studies in appendices
Practical utility as a drop-in replacement with negligible computational overhead (Table 1)
Clear presentation with well-motivated visualizations, particularly gradient variance analysis (Figure 5) and SNR correlation (Figure 6)
Loss-swap ablation (C.2) provides evidence that the cross-entropy objective itself contributes to performance gains beyond discretization alone
weaknesses: Limited novelty: combines existing techniques (discretized actors from Tang & Agrawal 2020, regularized networks from SimBa/BroNet) without significant innovation; explicitly chooses 'simplest baseline' rather than exploring advanced schemes

Weak theoretical justification: Proposition 4.1 assumes constant returns and vanilla REINFORCE without clipping/baselines (inapplicable to PPO); the cross-entropy argument is speculative without rigorous theory for why policy learning should benefit as value learning does
Confounded experimental design: RN-D combines discretization AND architectural improvements; unclear how much gain comes from regularization versus discretization specifically

Significant practical limitation: Performance is highly sensitive to bin count K with substantial degradation for large K and task-dependent optimal choices (C.4); treated as minor appendix issue despite being a major hyperparameter

Incremental empirical gains: Improvements are often modest (10-20% on locomotion), high variance on some tasks (HalfCheetah, Walker2d), greatly diminished on vision-based tasks (ManiSkill RGB); no statistical significance testing on individual tasks

Insufficient mechanistic analysis: Shows that discretization helps but provides limited insight beyond 'lower variance' and 'cross-entropy loss'; unexplained patterns like why StackCube gains are ~1.7× while HalfCheetah is modest

Missing comparisons to ordinal or unimodal discrete parameterizations (Zhu et al. 2024) despite acknowledgment; no guidance for practitioners on choosing K, residual block count N, or hidden dimension dh across different domains

strengths: Strong theoretical motivation with rigorous gradient variance analysis (Proposition 4.1) showing categorical policies have bounded variance while Gaussian policies scale with σ^{-2}
Comprehensive experimental validation across 20 diverse tasks (Gym, ManiSkill state-based and vision-based), multiple algorithms (PPO, TRPO, SPO), with proper statistical reporting (95% CI, 5 seeds)
Well-designed loss-swap ablation (C.2) convincingly demonstrates the cross-entropy objective is crucial—not just action discretization
Simple, practical drop-in replacement with no computational overhead (Table 1) and clear reproducibility support with comprehensive hyperparameter documentation
Thorough ablations isolating architectural components (Figure 6), network capacity effects (C.3), discretization granularity (C.4), enabling sound empirical conclusions
Consistent 1.3–1.9× sample efficiency improvements across diverse benchmarks demonstrating algorithm-agnostic benefits
Clear presentation connecting policy objectives to supervised learning principles (MSE vs. cross-entropy) with intuitive visualizations

Theoretical analysis limited to toy REINFORCE setting with constant rewards; doesn't account for PPO clipping, advantage normalization, or how these interact with categorical policy optimization
No formal justification for why regularized network architecture specifically benefits categorical actors beyond general optimization principles
